warmup.q: A Kotlin adapter implements fun interface Courier { fun book(address: String): String } and calls an old client method that throws IOException, with no try/catch. What happens when the old client throws?
options: It doesn't compile: the IOException must be caught or declared
The IOException travels straight through the port to whoever called book
The exception is swallowed and book returns an empty string
warmup.why: Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so the code compiles, and the client's IOException reaches the shop's code through a port that never mentioned it. In Java the same adapter wouldn't compile, because the port's method doesn't declare IOException. So in Kotlin, translating foreign errors at the edge is a habit you have to keep yourself. The first section's Try it shows both languages side by side.

opening:
You arrive at a hotel in another country with a phone charger from home. The socket in the wall has the wrong shape, so you push a travel plug adapter into it. The socket stays the same, the charger stays the same, and the little block in between makes them fit. Downstairs, the reception desk does a different job. You ask for breakfast at seven and fresh towels, and the desk talks to the kitchen and to housekeeping for you.

The corner shop needs both kinds of help. Its warehouse runs an old program, bought years ago, that speaks in item numbers and two-digit codes. And placing one order takes several steps across several parts of the program. The easy trap is to let the old program's codes leak into every class, and to let every caller repeat the steps in its own slightly different order.

In the last lesson, we built our own objects. In this lesson, we'll fit someone else's: an adapter that keeps an old program's words to itself, Kotlin's extension functions as light adapters, and a facade, one front desk for a job with several steps. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started in a hotel with a travel plug and a reception desk. In the shop, the plug became an adapter that keeps the old warehouse program's codes to itself. The desk became one call that reserves, writes down and tells the customer, in the right order.

Now look in your own code for an outside system's words outside its adapter: a status code compared as a string, or a library's exception caught far from the call that threw it. Each one is foreign voltage leaking past the plug.

Next, we'll wrap an object and keep its interface exactly as it is. What can a wrapper add when it doesn't change the shape at all?

sections.h: Adapter: make their interface fit your port
sections.html:
An adapter makes a class you can't change fit the interface your code expects. That's the travel plug: the hotel's socket is the class you can't change, your charger is your own code, and the adapter sits between them.

The first thing the shop has to fit is a courier company's old client library. It speaks XML, a text format of tags in angle brackets, and it throws IOException when the courier's office is closed. IOException is a checked exception, one the Java compiler makes you catch or declare. The shop's code should see none of that. It should see its own port: an interface, in the shop's own words, that the rest of the code depends on.

Java
interface Courier {
    String book(String address, int grams);
}
Kotlin
fun interface Courier {
    fun book(address: String, grams: Int): String
}

The adapter implements the port and holds the old client. All the translation happens inside it, in both directions: the shop's words into the client's on the way in, and the client's answers and errors into the shop's on the way out.

Java
record OldCourierAdapter(OldCourierClient old) implements Courier {
    public String book(String address, int grams) {
        String xml = "<parcel grams='" + grams + "' to='" + address + "'/>";
        try {
            String answer = old.submit(xml);
            return answer.substring(answer.indexOf("ref='") + 5, answer.lastIndexOf("'"));   // their format ends here
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new CourierUnavailable("courier unreachable", e);                          // our exception, not theirs
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
class OldCourierAdapter(private val old: OldCourierClient) : Courier {
    override fun book(address: String, grams: Int): String {
        val xml = "<parcel grams='$grams' to='$address'/>"
        try {
            val answer = old.submit(xml)
            return answer.substringAfter("ref='").substringBefore("'")         // their format ends here
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            throw CourierUnavailable("courier unreachable", e)                 // our exception, not theirs
        }
    }
}

First we write the request in their format, then we call them, then we cut our booking reference out of their answer. The tricky line is the catch. Their IOException stops there, and the caller gets the shop's own CourierUnavailable instead. XmlAdapterDemo, in the Try it, books one parcel and then tries an address the courier can't reach:

booked, ref R-2500
caller sees CourierUnavailable: courier unreachable
lambda adapter: QUICK-990

The most common adapter bug is a leaky one. If IOException, the old client's codes or its classes show up in the shop's other classes, every caller now depends on that courier. Switching couriers then means changing all of them. That's where the travel plug picture breaks. A plug either fits or it doesn't, but a software adapter must also translate failures. A leaky one passes the foreign voltage straight through.

Java's checked exceptions help here, almost by accident. The port doesn't declare IOException, so the Java compiler won't let the client's exception escape the adapter. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so the same leak compiles without a word. In Kotlin, the discipline is yours.

Translate at the edge, in both directions. Let nothing foreign through.

When the port has one method, as Courier does, you don't even need a class. A lambda or a method reference is the adapter, in both languages, and that's the third line of the output. For plain data, Kotlin has a lighter adapter still.

try.title: Let the old client's exception leak
steps: Run XmlAdapterDemo in either language with the command below. Read the three lines.
In the Java version, delete the try/catch in OldCourierAdapter.book, keeping the two lines inside the try. Predict, then run.
Do the same in the Kotlin version. Predict, then run. Restore both files.

code.title: XmlAdapterDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l04; import java.io.IOException; import java.util.function.BiFunction; /** An old courier client adapted to our port, plus a lambda adapter for a one-method port. */ public class XmlAdapterDemo { // the port our shop code depends on interface Courier { String book(String address, int grams); } // a client we can't change: XML text in, XML text out, checked IOException on failure static final class OldCourierClient { String submit(String xml) throws IOException { if (xml.contains("Nowhere")) throw new IOException("courier office closed: 503"); String grams = xml.substring(xml.indexOf("grams='") + 7, xml.indexOf("' to=")); return "<ok ref='R-" + grams + "'/>"; } } static final class CourierUnavailable extends RuntimeException { CourierUnavailable(String message, Throwable cause) { super(message, cause); } } // the adapter: implements our port, holds the old client, translates both ways record OldCourierAdapter(OldCourierClient old) implements Courier { public String book(String address, int grams) { String xml = "<parcel grams='" + grams + "' to='" + address + "'/>"; try { String answer = old.submit(xml); return answer.substring(answer.indexOf("ref='") + 5, answer.lastIndexOf("'")); // their format ends here } catch (IOException e) { throw new CourierUnavailable("courier unreachable", e); // our exception, not theirs } } } // for a one-method port, a lambda is the adapter static Courier fromFunction(BiFunction<String, Integer, String> oldBook) { return (address, grams) -> oldBook.apply(address, grams); } public static void main(String[] args) { Courier courier = new OldCourierAdapter(new OldCourierClient()); System.out.println("booked, ref " + courier.book("12 Mill Lane", 2_500)); try { courier.book("1 Nowhere Road", 2_500); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("caller sees " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage()); } Courier quick = fromFunction((address, grams) -> "QUICK-" + grams); System.out.println("lambda adapter: " + quick.book("3 Pier Street", 990)); } }

alt.title: XmlAdapterDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l04 import java.io.IOException // An old courier client adapted to our port, plus a lambda adapter for a one-method port. // the port our shop code depends on fun interface Courier { fun book(address: String, grams: Int): String } // a client we can't change: XML text in, XML text out, IOException on failure class OldCourierClient { @Throws(IOException::class) fun submit(xml: String): String { if ("Nowhere" in xml) throw IOException("courier office closed: 503") val grams = xml.substringAfter("grams='").substringBefore("' to=") return "<ok ref='R-$grams'/>" } } class CourierUnavailable(message: String, cause: Throwable) : RuntimeException(message, cause) // the adapter: implements our port, holds the old client, translates both ways class OldCourierAdapter(private val old: OldCourierClient) : Courier { override fun book(address: String, grams: Int): String { val xml = "<parcel grams='$grams' to='$address'/>" try { val answer = old.submit(xml) return answer.substringAfter("ref='").substringBefore("'") // their format ends here } catch (e: IOException) { throw CourierUnavailable("courier unreachable", e) // our exception, not theirs } } } fun main() { val courier: Courier = OldCourierAdapter(OldCourierClient()) println("booked, ref " + courier.book("12 Mill Lane", 2_500)) try { courier.book("1 Nowhere Road", 2_500) } catch (e: Exception) { println("caller sees ${e.javaClass.simpleName}: ${e.message}") } // for a fun interface, a lambda is the adapter (SAM conversion) val quick = Courier { _, grams -> "QUICK-$grams" } println("lambda adapter: " + quick.book("3 Pier Street", 990)) }

try.expect: Both versions print booked, ref R-2500, caller sees CourierUnavailable: courier unreachable and lambda adapter: QUICK-990. Without the catch, Java refuses to compile: unreported exception IOException; must be caught or declared to be thrown. Kotlin compiles and prints caller sees IOException: courier office closed: 503: the old client's exception walked straight through your port.

sections.h: Extension functions are Kotlin's light adapters
sections.html:
The shop buys tea and spices from a supplier abroad. The supplier's price list arrives as rows with the supplier's own names: qty, unit and avail. One of its units is the pound (LB), while the shop weighs everything in grams. We want our own Product. Write the mapping once, as an extension on the supplier's type:

Java
// Java has no extension functions: the same adapter is a static method
static Product toProduct(SupplierItem item) {
    double perUnit = switch (item.unit()) {
        case "KG" -> 1_000.0;
        case "LB" -> 453.59237;                 // the supplier abroad still weighs in pounds
        default -> throw new IllegalStateException("unknown unit " + item.unit());
    };
    return new Product(item.code(),
            Math.round(Double.parseDouble(item.qty()) * perUnit),
            item.avail().equals("Y"));
}

List<Product> products = fromSupplier.stream().map(Adapters::toProduct).toList();
Kotlin
fun SupplierItem.toProduct(): Product {
    val perUnit = when (unit) {
        "KG" -> 1_000.0
        "LB" -> 453.59237                       // the supplier abroad still weighs in pounds
        else -> error("unknown unit $unit")
    }
    return Product(
        code = code,
        grams = (qty.toDouble() * perUnit).roundToLong(),
        inStock = avail == "Y",
    )
}

val products = fromSupplier.map { it.toProduct() }

An extension function lets you call a function as if it were a method of a type you don't own. It isn't part of the class. It compiles to a static method that takes the receiver, the object before the dot, as its first parameter, which is exactly the Java twin. What changes is how the call reads, item.toProduct(), and where the editor offers it: type item. and it appears next to the supplier's own properties. The demo printed:

Product(code=T-1001, grams=2500, inStock=true)
Product(code=T-1002, grams=680, inStock=true)
Product(code=T-1003, grams=10000, inStock=false)

The 1.5 pounds came in as 680 grams, and the rest of the shop never has to know that pounds exist. That's the plug adapter at its simplest: the same thing in a different shape, translated once, at the edge.

Two rules keep these adapters honest. Keep them next to the code that talks to the supplier, not in a shared utils file, because they're part of the translation layer. And use them for data, not for behavior. An extension can't hold state, can't implement your port, and can't be swapped for a fake in a test. When you need something your code depends on, write a port and a class.

Extensions translate data. Ports and classes carry behavior.

The other light adapter in Kotlin is the fun interface, an interface with one method that a lambda can implement. Courier { _, grams -> "QUICK-$grams" } built the third line of the first section's output, the same way a Java lambda implements an interface with one method.

So far each adapter wraps one thing. Placing an order touches several.

try.title: Turn a supplier's rows into products
steps: Read ExtensionAdapters.kt (or its Java twin). Predict the three products, and look hard at the one in pounds.
Run it with the command below.
Add SupplierItem("T-1004", "0.5", "LB", "N") to the list (new SupplierItem(...) in Java) and predict its grams and inStock before you run.

code.title: ExtensionAdapters.kt
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l04 import kotlin.math.roundToLong // A row from a supplier's price list, with the supplier's names and units. class SupplierItem(val code: String, val qty: String, val unit: String, val avail: String) // Our own type. data class Product(val code: String, val grams: Long, val inStock: Boolean) // An extension function is a light adapter: it reads like a method on the supplier's type, // lives in our code, and keeps the mapping in one place. fun SupplierItem.toProduct(): Product { val perUnit = when (unit) { "KG" -> 1_000.0 "LB" -> 453.59237 // the supplier abroad still weighs in pounds else -> error("unknown unit $unit") } return Product( code = code, grams = (qty.toDouble() * perUnit).roundToLong(), inStock = avail == "Y", ) } fun main() { val fromSupplier = listOf( SupplierItem("T-1001", "2.5", "KG", "Y"), SupplierItem("T-1002", "1.5", "LB", "Y"), SupplierItem("T-1003", "10", "KG", "N"), ) fromSupplier.map { it.toProduct() }.forEach(::println) }

alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l04; import java.util.List; /** The Java twin of ExtensionAdapters.kt. Java has no extension functions, so the adapter is a static method. */ public class ExtensionAdaptersJava { // a row from a supplier's price list, with the supplier's names and units record SupplierItem(String code, String qty, String unit, String avail) {} // our own type record Product(String code, long grams, boolean inStock) {} // callers write toProduct(item), not item.toProduct(); the mapping still lives in one place static Product toProduct(SupplierItem item) { double perUnit = switch (item.unit()) { case "KG" -> 1_000.0; case "LB" -> 453.59237; // the supplier abroad still weighs in pounds default -> throw new IllegalStateException("unknown unit " + item.unit()); }; return new Product( item.code(), Math.round(Double.parseDouble(item.qty()) * perUnit), item.avail().equals("Y")); } public static void main(String[] args) { List<SupplierItem> fromSupplier = List.of( new SupplierItem("T-1001", "2.5", "KG", "Y"), new SupplierItem("T-1002", "1.5", "LB", "Y"), new SupplierItem("T-1003", "10", "KG", "N")); fromSupplier.stream().map(ExtensionAdaptersJava::toProduct).forEach(System.out::println); } }

The Kotlin call site reads it.toProduct(), and the Java one reads toProduct(item). Underneath, both are the same static method.

sections.h: Facade: one front desk for a job with several steps
sections.html:
Back at the hotel, you asked the reception desk for breakfast at seven, and the desk did the rest. A facade is that desk in code: one simple entry point to a job that takes several parts of the program.

Placing an order at the corner shop takes three steps: reserve the stock, book a van, and tell the customer. If every caller (the website, the phone line, the shop counter) makes those calls itself, each one gets the order of the steps and the failure handling slightly different. Put the sequence in one class:

Java
record FrontDesk(Stock stock, Vans vans, Notifier notifier) {
    String order(String product, String address, String email) {
        if (!stock.reserve(product)) throw new IllegalStateException("out of stock: " + product);   // 1. reserve
        String booking;
        try {
            booking = vans.book(product, address);                                               // 2. book a van
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            stock.release(product);                                                              // 3. undo the reservation
            throw e;
        }
        notifier.send(email, "on its way, booking " + booking);                                  // 4. tell the customer
        return booking;
    }
}
Kotlin
class FrontDesk(
    private val stock: Stock,
    private val vans: Vans,
    private val notifier: Notifier,
) {
    fun order(product: String, address: String, email: String): String {
        check(stock.reserve(product)) { "out of stock: $product" }               // 1. reserve
        val booking = try {
            vans.book(product, address)                                         // 2. book a van
        } catch (e: RuntimeException) {
            stock.release(product)                                              // 3. undo the reservation
            throw e
        }
        notifier.send(email, "on its way, booking $booking")                    // 4. tell the customer
        return booking
    }
}

The desk owns two decisions: the order of the steps, and what a failure at each step means. Booking a van before reserving would send a van for flour the shop doesn't have. A van that can't go somewhere must give the stock back. FrontDeskDemo, in the Try it, places one order to Mill Lane and one to Gull Island, where no van goes:

booking: V-flour
failed: no van goes to Gull Island; still reserved: [flour]

The sugar for Gull Island went back on the shelf. Those rules now live in one tested place, and each caller is one line.

Nothing in either language replaces Facade. Records and constructor parameters only make it shorter. The risk is growth. A facade should orchestrate, that is, call the parts in the right order, and nothing else: no unit math and no warehouse codes. A front desk that also cooks, cleans and does the laundry is no longer a desk. It's the whole hotel with one door.

That's also where the picture breaks. A clerk can improvise when something new comes up, and a facade only knows the steps it was written with. When one grows to forty methods, split it by job, such as an OrderDesk and a ReturnsDesk.

A facade owns the order of the steps and the undo. Nothing else.

One Java gotcha showed up while writing this example. A record component can't be called notify. The Java compiler says "illegal record component name", because the accessor method notify() would clash with Object.notify(). The same goes for wait, hashCode, toString, getClass and the other Object methods that take no arguments. A Kotlin property named notify compiles to getNotify() and is fine.

We have adapters on the edge and a desk at the front. Let's put them on one picture.

try.title: Break the desk's undo rule
steps: Run FrontDeskDemo in either language, and read the still reserved line.
Remove the try/catch around the van booking, so a failed booking no longer gives the stock back. Predict the still reserved line, then run.
Restore it. In the Java version only, rename the record component notifier to notify (and its use inside order). Compile.

code.title: FrontDeskDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l04; import java.util.HashSet; import java.util.Set; /** A facade over stock, vans and messages: one call, the right order, cleanup on failure. */ public class FrontDeskDemo { interface Stock { boolean reserve(String product); void release(String product); } interface Vans { String book(String product, String address); } interface Notifier { void send(String to, String message); } record FrontDesk(Stock stock, Vans vans, Notifier notifier) { String order(String product, String address, String email) { if (!stock.reserve(product)) throw new IllegalStateException("out of stock: " + product); // 1. reserve String booking; try { booking = vans.book(product, address); // 2. book a van } catch (RuntimeException e) { stock.release(product); // 3. undo the reservation throw e; } notifier.send(email, "on its way, booking " + booking); // 4. tell the customer return booking; } } public static void main(String[] args) { Set<String> reserved = new HashSet<>(); Stock stock = new Stock() { public boolean reserve(String product) { return reserved.add(product); } public void release(String product) { reserved.remove(product); } }; Vans vans = (product, address) -> { if (address.contains("Island")) throw new IllegalStateException("no van goes to " + address); return "V-" + product; }; Notifier notifier = (to, message) -> System.out.println(" mail to " + to + ": " + message); FrontDesk desk = new FrontDesk(stock, vans, notifier); System.out.println("booking: " + desk.order("flour", "12 Mill Lane", "anna@example.com")); try { desk.order("sugar", "Gull Island", "ben@example.com"); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("failed: " + e.getMessage() + "; still reserved: " + reserved); } } }

alt.title: FrontDeskDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l04 // A facade over stock, vans and messages: one call, the right order, cleanup on failure. interface Stock { fun reserve(product: String): Boolean; fun release(product: String) } fun interface Vans { fun book(product: String, address: String): String } fun interface Notifier { fun send(to: String, message: String) } class FrontDesk( private val stock: Stock, private val vans: Vans, private val notifier: Notifier, ) { fun order(product: String, address: String, email: String): String { check(stock.reserve(product)) { "out of stock: $product" } // 1. reserve val booking = try { vans.book(product, address) // 2. book a van } catch (e: RuntimeException) { stock.release(product) // 3. undo the reservation throw e } notifier.send(email, "on its way, booking $booking") // 4. tell the customer return booking } } fun main() { val reserved = mutableSetOf<String>() val stock = object : Stock { override fun reserve(product: String) = reserved.add(product) override fun release(product: String) { reserved.remove(product) } } val vans = Vans { product, address -> check("Island" !in address) { "no van goes to $address" } "V-$product" } val notifier = Notifier { to, message -> println(" mail to $to: $message") } val desk = FrontDesk(stock, vans, notifier) println("booking: " + desk.order("flour", "12 Mill Lane", "anna@example.com")) try { desk.order("sugar", "Gull Island", "ben@example.com") } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("failed: ${e.message}; still reserved: $reserved") } }

try.expect: The first run mails a confirmation for the flour, then prints failed: no van goes to Gull Island; still reserved: [flour]: the failed order gave the sugar back. Without the catch, the line ends [flour, sugar], so a failed booking holds stock until someone notices. The rename gives error: illegal record component name notify. The Kotlin class can have a property called notify.

sections.h: Ports and adapters: where the translation lives
sections.html:
Adapter and Facade both wrap something, and so do Decorator, Proxy and Bridge, which you'll meet in the next two lessons. Their structure looks much the same, so intent tells them apart:

Pattern Wraps Offers Why
Adapter one object you can't change a different interface: yours make it fit your port
Facade several objects a new, simpler interface hide a sequence of calls
Decorator one object the same interface add behavior (Decorator and Proxy, lesson 5 of this track)
Proxy one object the same interface control access (lesson 5 of this track)
Bridge an implementation you pick your abstraction vary two things separately (lesson 6 of this track)

In a program built with ports and adapters, a layout often called hexagonal architecture, you see Adapter and Facade on one picture. The shop's own logic sits in the middle and talks only to ports: Warehouse, OrderBook, Notifier. Adapters sit on the edge, one for each outside system: the old warehouse program, a database, a mail server. The facade is the front door, where the website or the phone line makes one call. The figure shows the lab laid out this way.

That layout pays off twice. Switching warehouses means writing one new adapter, and nothing in the middle changes. And the middle can be tested with lambdas: new OrderDesk((product, grams) -> new Reserved("H1"), orderBook, notifier) needs no warehouse, no database and no mail server.

Domain-driven design, a well-known way of organizing business software, calls a thick layer of adapters an anti-corruption layer: the place where an outside system's model is translated into yours, so it never spreads. The shop's old warehouse program needs one. It answers every request with a two-digit code and a pipe (|), like a clerk who stopped speaking in full sentences years ago. 00|H4711 means "held, and here's the hold id", and 51| means "out of stock". If you find "51" anywhere outside the adapter, the layer has a hole.

The lab is that layer in miniature. WarehouseAdapter keeps the old program's item numbers, kilograms and codes to itself, and OrderDesk lets the website place an order without knowing the steps.

Keep foreign words at the edge. The middle speaks only your own.

Check yourself. The shop replaces its warehouse, and the new program throws TimeoutException where the old one threw WarehouseException. In a program laid out this way, which files change? (Only the new warehouse adapter, which catches the new exception and returns the same Unavailable. The desk, the shop's logic and their tests don't change, because they never saw WarehouseException either.)

figure.caption: Callers make one call to the desk. The shop's own code talks only to ports, and adapters on the edge translate for each outside system.

compare.title: An anti-corruption adapter for the courier's status messages

java.title: CourierUpdateAdapter.java
java.html: // the courier's status message, with the courier's names record CourierUpdate(String type, String ref, String info) {} // our model of what happened sealed interface DeliveryEvent { record Delivered(String bookingRef) implements DeliveryEvent {} record Missed(String bookingRef, String reason) implements DeliveryEvent {} record Ignored(String why) implements DeliveryEvent {} } final class CourierUpdateAdapter { private CourierUpdateAdapter() {} static DeliveryEvent toEvent(CourierUpdate u) { return switch (u.type()) { // their strings are an open set, so a default is right here case "parcel.delivered" -> new DeliveryEvent.Delivered(u.ref()); case "parcel.missed" -> new DeliveryEvent.Missed(u.ref(), u.info().toLowerCase()); default -> new DeliveryEvent.Ignored("unhandled courier update " + u.type()); }; } }

kotlin.title: CourierUpdateAdapter.kt
kotlin.html: // the courier's status message, with the courier's names data class CourierUpdate(val type: String, val ref: String, val info: String) // our model of what happened sealed interface DeliveryEvent { data class Delivered(val bookingRef: String) : DeliveryEvent data class Missed(val bookingRef: String, val reason: String) : DeliveryEvent data class Ignored(val why: String) : DeliveryEvent } // the adapter as an extension: reads like a method on the courier's type fun CourierUpdate.toEvent(): DeliveryEvent = when (type) { // an open set of their strings: else is right "parcel.delivered" -> DeliveryEvent.Delivered(ref) "parcel.missed" -> DeliveryEvent.Missed(ref, info.lowercase()) else -> DeliveryEvent.Ignored("unhandled courier update $type") }

compare.note: The courier's system sends a short status message whenever a parcel's state changes, in the courier's words. The translation is the same in both languages: their strings in, a sealed event of our own out. Kotlin writes it as an extension on their type, so call sites read update.toEvent(). Java needs a static method on a holder class, so call sites read CourierUpdateAdapter.toEvent(update), and in bytecode, the compiled form the JVM runs, the two are the same static method. Both use a catch-all branch on purpose. The courier's message types are an open set you don't control, unlike your own sealed types, where a missing case should break the build. Code that uses DeliveryEvent then switches over it with no default. Neither language makes Adapter unnecessary; Kotlin just makes the data-mapping kind cheaper to write.

worked.title: Wrap a map service behind a port, then test without it

steps.say: The shop prices a delivery by distance: 2.00 plus 0.50 for every kilometer. Its pricer calls an outside map service directly. The service answers with text like "dist=4.2km;eta=11min" and throws a checked RouteException. Before reading on, list every detail of the map service that leaks into priceCents.
steps.code: class DeliveryPricer { private final RouteClient routes = new RouteClient("https://maps.vendor.example"); long priceCents(String address) throws RouteException { String raw = routes.distance("SHOP", address); // their format: "dist=4.2km;eta=11min" double km = Double.parseDouble(raw.substring(raw.indexOf('=') + 1, raw.indexOf("km"))); return 200 + Math.round(km * 50); } }

alt.html: class DeliveryPricer { private val routes = RouteClient("https://maps.vendor.example") fun priceCents(address: String): Long { val raw = routes.distance("SHOP", address) // their format; RouteException leaks unseen val km = raw.substringAfter('=').substringBefore("km").toDouble() return 200 + (km * 50).roundToLong() } }

steps.say: Four leaks: the "SHOP" name the service wants, its answer format, its checked exception, and its hard-wired address. Define the port in the shop's words first. It says nothing about text formats or vendors, and an empty answer means "no distance right now".
steps.code: interface Distances { OptionalDouble km(String from, String to); // 1. our words: places in, kilometers or nothing out } class DeliveryPricer { private final Distances distances; DeliveryPricer(Distances distances) { this.distances = distances; } OptionalLong priceCents(String address) { OptionalDouble km = distances.km("SHOP", address); return km.isPresent() ? OptionalLong.of(200 + Math.round(km.getAsDouble() * 50)) : OptionalLong.empty(); } }

alt.html: fun interface Distances { fun km(from: String, to: String): Double? // 1. our words: places in, kilometers or null out } class DeliveryPricer(private val distances: Distances) { fun priceCents(address: String): Long? = distances.km("SHOP", address)?.let { 200 + (it * 50).roundToLong() } }

steps.say: Now the adapter. Everything the map service knows lives here: how it wants places named, how it packs its answers, and which exception it throws. Why return empty instead of rethrowing on RouteException? Because the port promised "kilometers or nothing", and the pricer decides what nothing means.
steps.code: final class MapDistances implements Distances { private final RouteClient routes; MapDistances(RouteClient routes) { this.routes = routes; } public OptionalDouble km(String from, String to) { try { String raw = routes.distance(from, to); // 2. our places, their format return OptionalDouble.of(Double.parseDouble(raw.substring(raw.indexOf('=') + 1, raw.indexOf("km")))); } catch (RouteException | RuntimeException e) { // 3. their failure, our answer return OptionalDouble.empty(); } } }

alt.html: class MapDistances(private val routes: RouteClient) : Distances { override fun km(from: String, to: String): Double? = try { val raw = routes.distance(from, to) // 2. our places, their format raw.substringAfter('=').substringBefore("km").toDouble() } catch (e: RouteException) { // 3. their failure, our answer null } catch (e: RuntimeException) { null } }

steps.say: Test the two halves separately. The pricer gets a lambda. The adapter gets a fake map service, a subclass of the client that returns a canned answer, which is how the lab tests its warehouse adapter.
steps.code: // 4. the shop's logic, with no map service at all assertThat(new DeliveryPricer((from, to) -> OptionalDouble.of(4.0)).priceCents("12 Mill Lane")).hasValue(400); // 5. the adapter, against a fake of the client class RouteClient fake = new RouteClient("unused") { @Override public String distance(String from, String to) { return "dist=4.2km;eta=11min"; } }; assertThat(new MapDistances(fake).km("SHOP", "12 Mill Lane")).hasValue(4.2);

alt.html: // 4. the shop's logic, with no map service at all assertThat(DeliveryPricer { _, _ -> 4.0 }.priceCents("12 Mill Lane")).isEqualTo(400L) // 5. the adapter, against a fake of the client class (open in the library, or use an interface) val fake = object : RouteClient("unused") { override fun distance(from: String, to: String) = "dist=4.2km;eta=11min" } assertThat(MapDistances(fake).km("SHOP", "12 Mill Lane")).isEqualTo(4.2)

lab.title: A warehouse adapter and an order desk
steps: Read OldWarehouseSystem.java (the old program you can't change), Warehouse.java (the shop's port) and Units.java (two helpers). They're given; don't edit them. Run the tests: all ten fail.

Write WarehouseAdapter.reserve. Call old.hold with Units.itemNumber and Units.toKilos, catch WarehouseException and return Unavailable(e.getMessage()), then split the answer on | and map the code with a switch.

Write OrderDesk.place as a switch over the StockResult. Reserved: write it in the order book, send the confirmation (catching a failing notifier), and return Placed. Refused: send the sorry note and return Refused. Unavailable: return RetryLater.
Run the tests until all ten pass.
hints: raw.split("\\|", -1) splits on a real | and keeps the empty hold id in "51|". The pipe must be escaped, because split takes a regular expression.
A switch over the sealed StockResult with case StockResult.Reserved ok -> ... needs no default: the compiler checks all three cases. In a switch expression, use yield to return a value from a block.
Wrap only the notifier call in try/catch. If the order book throws, let it travel up: a reserved order that isn't written down is a problem someone must see, not one to hide.

drill.title: An adapter from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. An outside PostcodeClient has String lookup(String postcode) throws LookupException, returning text like "Mill Lane;OLD TOWN". Your port is interface DistrictOf { Optional<String> district(String postcode); } (in Kotlin, fun interface DistrictOf { fun district(postcode: String): String? }). Write the adapter so the client's exception never escapes, and an empty or malformed answer gives no district.

answer.html: final class PostcodeDistricts implements DistrictOf { private final PostcodeClient client; PostcodeDistricts(PostcodeClient client) { this.client = client; } @Override public Optional<String> district(String postcode) { try { String raw = client.lookup(postcode); // their format: "Mill Lane;OLD TOWN" if (raw == null) return Optional.empty(); String[] parts = raw.split(";", 2); if (parts.length < 2 || parts[1].isBlank()) return Optional.empty(); return Optional.of(parts[1].trim()); } catch (LookupException e) { return Optional.empty(); // their failure stops here } } }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: class PostcodeDistricts(private val client: PostcodeClient) : DistrictOf { override fun district(postcode: String): String? = try { client.lookup(postcode) // their format: "Mill Lane;OLD TOWN" ?.split(';', limit = 2) ?.getOrNull(1) ?.trim() ?.takeIf { it.isNotEmpty() } } catch (e: LookupException) { null // their failure stops here } }

recap: An adapter makes a class you can't change fit your port. It translates arguments on the way in, and answers and errors on the way out.

Keep an outside system's types, codes and exceptions inside its adapter. A "51" or a WarehouseException anywhere else is a leak. Java's checked exceptions stop an IOException from escaping a port that doesn't declare it; Kotlin compiles the same leak without a word.
For a one-method port, a lambda or a fun interface is the adapter. For data, a Kotlin extension such as SupplierItem.toProduct() is the light adapter; in Java it's a static method.
A facade gives callers one call for a job with several steps, and owns the order of the steps and what each failure means. Keep it to orchestration only.
In ports and adapters, the shop's logic talks only to ports, adapters on the edge translate, and the facade is the front door.
The limit: neither pattern makes an outside system reliable. An adapter can only translate the failures it knows about, and a facade only knows the steps it was written with.

explain.prompt: Explain to a new teammate why WarehouseAdapter returns Unavailable instead of letting WarehouseException through, and why OrderDesk ignores a failing confirmation email but not a failing order-book write.
explain.answer: The adapter is the only class allowed to know the old warehouse program. If WarehouseException escaped, every caller would import the old program's type and make decisions on its status codes, and replacing the warehouse would mean changing all of them. So the adapter turns it into our own result, Unavailable, and the desk turns that into RetryLater. In the desk, the order matters. Once the stock is reserved, the order must be written down, so if the order book fails, that's a problem someone must see, and it travels up. The confirmation email is a courtesy. A broken mail server shouldn't turn a placed order into an error the customer retries, which could reserve the stock twice.

deeper.html:
The JDK has adapters you use every day. InputStreamReader adapts a stream of bytes into a stream of characters; its Javadoc calls it a bridge from byte streams to character streams, which shows how loosely the pattern names get used. Arrays.asList adapts an array into a fixed-size List that writes through to the array. Collections.enumeration and Enumeration.asIterator() (Java 9) adapt between the old and new ways of walking through a collection.

The GoF book describes two kinds of adapter. An object adapter holds the foreign object and delegates to it, as in this lesson. A class adapter inherits from the foreign class and implements your interface at the same time. Java and Kotlin allow the second only when the foreign class is open to subclassing, and it's usually worse: your adapter inherits every public method of the foreign class, so callers can go around your translation. Prefer the object adapter.

Kotlin's by delegation (in Decorator and Proxy, lesson 5 of this track) can build an adapter that forwards most of an interface unchanged and overrides the few methods that need translating. That works when the two interfaces are almost the same, such as two versions of your own API. For an outside system with a different model, write the translation out; it's the part that deserves a careful review.

Facades and slow calls mix badly in one way. Suppose a facade starts a database transaction, a group of database changes that succeed or fail together, and then calls a slow outside system inside it. The transaction holds a database connection for as long as the outside system takes. With a pool of 20 connections and a courier service that takes 120 ms to answer, a busy afternoon runs out of connections. Call the slow system first, outside the transaction, then write to the database in a short one.
